idiom_name: Sorbet sealed! module + T::Struct cases + T.absurd
implementation_notes: Ruby itself has no static types and no way to close a hierarchy, so the pattern is realized through Sorbet: a sealed! module (or abstract! + sealed! class) may only be included by classes defined in the same file, which is the closed variant set; each case is a T::Struct (or T::Enum) carrying its own props; and the consumer is a case/when whose else branch calls T.absurd(state), which turns a missing variant into a type error and raises if it is ever reached at run time. Without a checker the same code is only a convention - value classes (Data.define) and manual case/when can model the shapes but nothing prevents an illegal combination. Where the model is not type-checked, validate at the boundary and keep every construction in one factory.
code_sketch:
module ConnectionState
  extend T::Helpers
  sealed!                    # only classes in THIS file may include it
  class Disconnected < T::Struct; include ConnectionState; end
  class Connected < T::Struct; include ConnectionState; const :session_id, String; end
end

case state
when ConnectionState::Disconnected then "down"
when ConnectionState::Connected then state.session_id
else T.absurd(state)       # srb reports a missing case as a type error
end
pitfalls: T.absurd only proves exhaustiveness when Sorbet actually runs (srb tc in CI); at run time it raises, so a missing case ships as an exception rather than a compile failure if the check is skipped.
sealed! is file-scoped: every variant must be defined in the same file as the sealed module, which pushes the whole model into one file and makes 'adding a variant elsewhere' impossible by design.
T::Struct props are not runtime-validated and T::Enum values are process-wide singletons: validate in the constructor/factory and never put mutable state on an enum value.
